Meaning and scope of each writ
Habeas Corpus: 'to have the body'; order to produce detained person; examine legality; set free if illegal

Mandamus: 'we command'; command to public official to perform duties failed/refused

Prohibition: 'to forbid'; higher court to lower court/tribunal to prevent exceeding jurisdiction

Certiorari: 'to be certified'; higher court to lower court/tribunal to transfer case or quash order

Quo-Warranto: 'by what authority'; enquire into legality of claim to public office; prevents illegal usurpation

Not for ministerial or private office
Can be sought by any interested person, not necessarily aggrieved

Saving of Laws Giving Effect to Certain Directive Principles (Article 31C)
Inserted by 25th Amendment Act 1971

Criticism of Fundamental Rights
Excessive limitations: subjected to numerous exceptions, restrictions, qualifications
Jaspat Roy Kapoor suggestion: rename chapter as 'Limitations on Fundamental Rights' or 'Fundamental Rights and Limitations Thereon'
No social and economic rights: no right to social security, work, employment, rest, leisure
Provided in advanced democracies and socialistic constitutions
No clarity: vague, indefinite, ambiguous phrases like 'public order', 'minorities', 'reasonable restriction', 'public interest'
Language complicated, beyond common man; made by lawyers for lawyers
Sir Ivor Jennings called Constitution 'paradise for lawyers'
No permanency: Parliament can curtail or abolish; example: abolition of property right in 1978
Only limitation is doctrine of basic structure
Suspension during Emergency: enforcement suspended except Articles 20, 21; cuts at roots of democracy
Expensive remedy: judiciary too expensive for common man; rights benefit rich
Preventive detention (Article 22) takes away spirit; confers arbitrary powers
No consistent philosophy: not product of philosophical principle; creates difficulty for courts
